summary: A messenger who brings a get from outside Eretz Yisrael must say that it was written and signed in front of him. The Rabbis argue about which places need this.

chunks.en: Someone who brings a get from a faraway land overseas,

The "land of the sea" means any place outside Eretz Yisrael.

summary: Inside Eretz Yisrael, a messenger does not need to say the get was written and signed before him. If someone says the get is fake, the court checks the signatures of the witnesses.

chunks.st: One who brings a bill of divorce from one place to another within Eretz Yisrael

chunks.en: it is proven good through the signatures of its witnesses.
chunks.st: it should be ratified through its signatories.

summary: A document signed by a Kusi (Samaritan) witness, or made in a non-Jewish court, is usually still good. But a get and a slave's freeing paper are different, and Rabbi Shimon disagrees about the court papers.

chunks.he: כָּל גֵּט שֶׁיֵּשׁ עָלָיו עֵד כּוּתִי,
chunks.en: Any document with a Kusi witness signed on it
chunks.st: Any document that has a Samaritan witness signed on it

words.note: The Kusim (Samaritans) lived in Eretz Yisrael and kept only some of the Torah.

summary: If a man sends a get or a slave's freeing paper with a messenger, can he change his mind? The mishnah also teaches what happens if he dies before it is given.

chunks.en: Someone who says, "Give this get to my wife,
chunks.st: With regard to one who says to another: Give this bill of divorce to my wife,

chunks.en: and this freeing paper to my slave,"
chunks.st: or: Give this bill of manumission to my slave,

chunks.en: if he wants to change his mind about both of them,
chunks.st: if before the document reaches the woman or the slave the giver wishes to retract

chunks.en: he may take it back. These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
chunks.st: with regard to both of them, he can retract. This is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: And the Sages say,
chunks.st: And the Rabbis say:

chunks.en: he can take back a get for a woman,
chunks.st: One can retract his decision in the case of bills of divorce

chunks.en: but not a paper freeing a slave,
chunks.st: but not in the case of bills of manumission.
chunks.stMore: The Rabbis explain the reason for their ruling:

chunks.en: because we can do something good for a person even when he is not there,
chunks.explain: Going free is good for the slave, so the messenger takes it for him right away.
chunks.st: This is because one can act in a person’s interest in his absence,
chunks.stMore: and therefore the agent acquires the document on behalf of the slave from the moment the owner hands the bill of manumission to the agent.

chunks.en: but we may do something bad for him only when he is there.
chunks.explain: Getting a get is not good for the wife, so this needs her.
chunks.st: But one can act to a person’s detriment only in his presence.
chunks.stMore: The receipt of a bill of divorce is considered to be to a woman’s detriment, and therefore an agent cannot receive it for her without her consent. They explain further: The emancipation of a slave is in his interests, despite the fact that he receives sustenance from his master while a slave,

chunks.he: שֶׁאִם יִרְצֶה שֶׁלֹּא לָזוּן אֶת עַבְדּוֹ,
chunks.en: For if a master wants not to feed his slave,
chunks.st: as, if the master wishes not to sustain his slave

chunks.en: he is allowed. But not to feed his wife,
chunks.st: he is allowed
chunks.stMore: not to provide him with sustenance. This demonstrates that slavery is not in the interest of the slave, as he does not receive any guaranteed benefit. But if a husband wishes not to sustain his wife,

chunks.en: he is not allowed.
chunks.st: he is not allowed
chunks.stMore: to proceed in this manner. Consequently, marriage is in the interests of the woman.

chunks.en: Rabbi Meir said to them,
chunks.st: Rabbi Meir said to the Rabbis:

chunks.en: but he makes his slave lose the right to eat
chunks.st: But even so, it is not in the interest of a slave to be emancipated, as, if his master is a priest, he disqualifies his slave from

chunks.he: הַתְּרוּמָה כְּשֵׁם שֶׁהוּא פוֹסֵל אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ.
chunks.en: terumah, just as he makes his wife lose it.
chunks.explain: A Kohen's slave may eat terumah; once freed, he may not.
chunks.st: partaking of teruma by emancipating him, just as a husband who is a priest disqualifies his Israelite wife from partaking of teruma by divorcing her.

words.note: Terumah is a special food gift for Kohanim and their household.

chunks.en: They said to him,
chunks.st: The Rabbis said to him:

chunks.en: that is because the slave belongs to him.
chunks.st: It is permitted for a priest’s slave to partake of teruma not because he has a right to sustenance, but rather because he is his master’s acquisition.

chunks.en: Someone who says, "Give this get to my wife,
chunks.st: In the case of one who says: Give this bill of divorce to my wife,

chunks.en: and this freeing paper to my slave,"
chunks.st: or: Give this bill of manumission to my slave,

chunks.en: and then he died, they do not give them after his death.
chunks.st: and then he dies, one does not give it after his death.
chunks.stMore: The reason for this is that bills of divorce and manumission must be transferred by the husband or the master. Once he has died the document can no longer be given, and the agency he appointed for this purpose is likewise canceled.

chunks.en: But if he said, "Give a maneh to so-and-so,"
chunks.explain: A maneh is one hundred silver coins.
chunks.st: However, if he said: Give one hundred dinars to so-and-so,

chunks.en: and he died, they do give it after his death.
chunks.st: and then he died, one does give the recipient the money after his death.
